8.4.5 RESPIRATORY SYSTEM Organs coordinated for the intake and supply of oxygen to the tissues and throwing out carbon dioxide from the body constitute respiratory system. The entire process of respiration consists of mechanical and chemical processes such as inhaling oxygen and exhaling carbon dioxide, transport of gases and oxidation of food in the tissues to release energy. Tadpole or larva of frog lives completely in water and breathes through four pairs of external gills. Such respiration is called branchial respiration whereas Adult Frog spends dual or amphibious mode of life and performs respiration by the following ways:
1. Cutaneous respiration (through moist skin) 2. Buccopharyngeal respiration (through buccopharyngeal lining) 3. Pulmonary respiration (through lungs)

1. Cutaneous respiration: This type of respiration occurs all the time whether the frog is on land or in water. When the frog is metabolically less active and demand of oxygen is low or at the time of hibernation and aestivation; cutaneous respiration takes place. Skin of frog is very thin, moist, highly vascularized and an efficient organ for cutaneous respiration. It maintains skin moist by frequently visiting water sources and secreting slippery mucus by mucous gland present in its skin.

Figure 8.4.24 Cutaneous respiration in frog During gaseous exchange through skin, oxygen first dissolves in the thin layer of water covering the skin and diffuses through the epidermis into the blood capillaries present in the dermis. Then, oxygen is carried by the blood in the form of oxyhaemoglobin to the tissues and oxy-haemoglobin dissociates into oxygen and haemoglobin near the tissues. Oxygen diffuses into the cell. Oxygen is used for oxidation of glucose in the cell and carbon-dioxide is the waste product produced due to this process which is also carried by blood to the skin surface and then gets diffused out. 2. Bucco-pharyngeal respiration: This type of respiration takes place through the lining (internal layer) of bucco-pharyngeal cavity when the frog is resting on land or partially immersed in water. The inner lining of Biology, Grade 11 | 415

bucco-pharyngeal cavity is moist and richly supplied with blood capillaries. Hence, it serves as the respiratory surface for exchange of gases. Bucco-pharyngeal respiration takes place with the help two sets of muscles called sternohyal muscle and petrohyal muscles. Sternohyal muscles are those muscles, connected with sternum and hyoid whereas petrohyal muscles are connected with squamosal and hyoid bone. Contraction of sternohyal muscles lowers the floor of buccal cavity and contraction of petrohyal muscle raises the floor of buccal cavity. Process of inspiration and expiration in buccal respiration is discussed below. i. Inspiration
• At first, sternohyal muscle contracts and floor of buccal cavity is lowered. • Then, volume of buccal cavity increases and air pressure in the buccal cavity

decreases. • Air from outside, rushes into the cavity through nostrils. • Gullet, glottis and mouth remain closed during this process and no air passes into lungs. • Fresh air or oxygen diffuses through mucous layer (inner layer) of buccal cavity and passed into blood capillaries Figure 8.4.25 Inspiration in bucco pharyngeal respiration • Meanwhile, CO2 diffuses into the buccopharyngeal cavity from blood capillaries. ii. Expiration • Sternohyal muscle relaxes, petrohyal muscle contracts and floor of buccal cavity is raised. • Consequently, volume of buccal cavity decreases and air pressure increases in the buccal cavity. • Then air rich in carbondioxide, from buccal cavity escapes out through nostrils.
